title: AS Paper 2 mock — Set B: Productivity, growth and supply-side policy
description: A full 80-mark AS Paper 2 (Theme 2: The UK economy, performance and policies) to be sat in 90 minutes. Section A has four multiple-choice and four short-answer questions on SRAS, injections and withdrawals, macroeconomic objectives, the balance of payments, measuring living standards, consumption, automatic stabilisers and migration (aim for about 20-25 minutes). Section B is a data response on a fictional economy's productivity problem and Growth Plan, covering actual and potential growth, net investment, LRAS, equilibrium national output, the impact of growth and supply-side policies (about 65 minutes). Designed to complement Set A so the two papers together cover all of Theme 2. Show calculations, use AD/AS diagrams, and finish every 8+ mark answer with a justified judgement.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would cause a movement along the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve rather than a shift of it?
options: A A rise in the National Living Wage
B An increase in aggregate demand that raises the price level
C A fall in world oil prices
D An increase in the standard rate of VAT
questions.explanation: The SRAS curve shows how much firms will supply at each price level, holding costs constant. A shift in AD changes the price level, so firms move along SRAS (an extension when the price level rises). A, C and D change firms' costs of production at every price level, so they shift SRAS (A and D to the left, C to the right).

questions.prompt:
The table shows planned injections and withdrawals in an economy.

Item | £ billion
Investment | 40
Government spending | 90
Exports | 70
Saving | 50
Taxation | 85
Imports | 80

What is likely to happen to the level of national income?
options: A It will rise, because injections exceed withdrawals by £15 billion.
B It will fall, because withdrawals exceed injections by £15 billion.
C It will stay the same, because exports are close to imports.
D It will rise, because government spending exceeds taxation by £5 billion.
questions.explanation: Injections = I + G + X = 40 + 90 + 70 = £200 billion. Withdrawals = S + T + M = 50 + 85 + 80 = £215 billion. Withdrawals exceed injections by £15 billion, so less is flowing back into the circular flow than is leaking out and national income falls until withdrawals equal injections. D looks only at the government sector, ignoring the overall balance.

questions.prompt: Which of the following indicators would be most useful in judging whether a government is meeting an objective of greater equality in the distribution of income?
options: C The rate of CPI inflation
D The current account balance as a percentage of GDP
questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient measures how unequally income is distributed, from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person receives all income), so a fall indicates greater equality. Real GDP per capita (B) is an average and says nothing about distribution; C and D measure other macroeconomic objectives.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would be recorded as an outflow (debit) in the primary income section of the UK current account?
options: A Dividends paid by a UK company to shareholders living in the USA
B Insurance services sold by a London firm to a client in Germany
C UK government contributions to international aid programmes
D A Japanese firm buying a factory in the north-east of England
questions.explanation: Primary income covers income from investment and employment, such as profits, dividends and interest. Dividends paid to overseas shareholders are an outflow of primary income. B is an export of services (an inflow in the trade in services). C is a secondary income (current transfer) outflow. D is foreign direct investment, recorded in the financial account.

questions.prompt: Explain two limitations of using real GDP per capita to compare living standards between two countries.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Real GDP per capita is the value of a country's output adjusted for inflation, divided by its population; it is used as an indicator of average material living standards.
Application/Analysis (any two): It is an average, so it hides the distribution of income; a country with high inequality may have a higher figure but lower living standards for most people. It excludes the informal or hidden economy and unpaid work (such as caring), which may be larger in one country than another. It ignores non-material aspects of well-being such as leisure time, health, pollution and political freedom, which is why measures of national happiness or the HDI are also used. Converting at market exchange rates does not reflect differences in the cost of living, so comparisons should use purchasing power parity (PPP). Data quality and collection methods differ between countries.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge (definition of real GDP per capita or living standards); 1 mark for identifying each of two relevant limitations (max 2); 1 mark for developing either limitation, explaining how it could make a comparison between two countries misleading.

questions.prompt: Explain how a sustained rise in house prices may affect consumer spending in the UK.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: The wealth effect: an increase in the value of households' assets increases their wealth, which tends to increase consumption. Consumption is also influenced by confidence and access to credit.
Application: For many UK owner-occupiers their home is their largest asset, so rising house prices raise their wealth significantly.
Analysis: Homeowners feel wealthier and more confident, so they save a smaller proportion of income (the savings ratio falls) and spend more. Higher house values also increase the equity households can borrow against, so they may remortgage to fund spending on cars, holidays or home improvements. Spending on goods linked to moving home (furniture, appliances) may rise as transactions increase. Credit a developed counter-chain: renters and first-time buyers must save more for a larger deposit, which reduces their consumption.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge (the wealth effect or a definition of consumption); 1 mark for application to UK households; up to 2 marks for analysis (linked chains via confidence, saving, borrowing against housing equity, or the effect on first-time buyers).

questions.prompt: Explain how automatic stabilisers cause government spending and tax revenue to change during a recession.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Automatic stabilisers are changes in government spending and taxation that happen automatically as the economy moves through the trade cycle, without any new policy decision.
Application/Analysis: Government spending rises: as unemployment increases, more people become eligible for welfare payments such as Universal Credit, so transfer payments increase. Tax revenue falls: with lower incomes, spending and profits, receipts from income tax, VAT and corporation tax fall; because income tax is progressive, revenue falls proportionately more than incomes. Effect: these changes cushion households' disposable income and limit the fall in consumption and AD, reducing the depth of the recession, while the budget deficit widens.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge (definition of automatic stabilisers); 1 mark for explaining the rise in government spending (welfare payments); 1 mark for explaining the fall in tax revenue; 1 mark for explaining the stabilising effect on AD or the widening budget deficit.

questions.prompt: Explain two ways in which net inward migration of working-age people may affect the level of unemployment in an economy.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Net inward migration means more people entering a country to live than leaving it. Unemployment is the number of people of working age who are without work but actively seeking work.
Application/Analysis (any two, which may point in different directions): Larger labour supply: if migrants arrive faster than new jobs are created, competition for jobs may rise in some sectors or regions and unemployment may rise in the short run. Filling vacancies and skills shortages: migrants may take hard-to-fill jobs (for example in social care or construction), allowing firms to expand output, which creates further jobs for existing workers. Higher aggregate demand: migrants spend their incomes on housing, food and services, raising AD and the derived demand for labour, which reduces cyclical unemployment. Entrepreneurship: some migrants start businesses that employ others.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge (definition of net migration or unemployment); 1 mark for identifying each of two relevant effects (max 2); 1 mark for developing either effect with a clear chain of reasoning.

questions.prompt: Using Table 1, calculate the percentage change in real GDP per head in Norhaven between 2015 and 2025. Explain the difference between actual and potential economic growth.
questions.context:
Norhaven: in search of faster growth (illustrative data)

Table 1: Selected indicators for Norhaven, 2015-2025 (illustrative data)
Indicator | 2015 | 2020 | 2025
Real GDP (£ billion, 2020 prices) | 400 | 418 | 442
Population (millions) | 20.0 | 20.6 | 21.2
Output per hour worked (index, 2015 = 100) | 100 | 103 | 105
Gross investment (£ billion, 2020 prices) | 64 | 63 | 68
Depreciation of the capital stock (£ billion, 2020 prices) | 52 | 56 | 61
Spending on research and development (% of GDP) | 1.0 | 0.9 | 0.9
Unemployment, ILO (%) | 6.5 | 5.0 | 4.1

Table 2: Norhaven's regions, 2025 (illustrative data)
Region | GDP per head (£) | Adults with a degree or higher technical qualification (%)
Capital region | 30,000 | 52
Northern region | 16,500 | 27
Coastal region | 18,000 | 31

Extract A: Norhaven's productivity puzzle
Norhaven, a fictional economy, has grown steadily but slowly since 2015. Most of its growth has come from more people working rather than from each worker producing more: output per hour rose by only 5% in ten years, compared with around 15% in its main trading partners. Business surveys point to several causes. Net investment has been low, so many firms rely on ageing equipment; spending on research and development is below 1% of GDP; and employers report shortages of engineers, technicians and skilled construction workers. Planning rules make it slow and costly to build new factories, warehouses and homes, and transport links between the Northern region and the Capital region are poor. Unemployment is now low and firms say they are struggling to recruit.

Extract B: The Growth Plan
In its 2025 Budget the government announced a Growth Plan. Its market-based measures are: cutting the basic rate of income tax from 22% to 20%; cutting corporation tax from 28% to 25%; allowing firms to deduct the full cost of new machinery from taxable profits in the year it is bought; and simplifying planning rules. Its interventionist measures are: £3 billion a year for apprenticeships and technical colleges in the Northern and Coastal regions; a state-owned investment bank to lend to small firms; and £2 billion a year of extra public spending on research grants. The independent fiscal watchdog estimates that the plan will raise the economy's potential growth rate by between 0.2 and 0.4 percentage points a year after five years, but warns that the income tax cut will add to demand at a time when there is little spare capacity.

Extract C: Growth for whom?
Critics argue that the benefits of growth in Norhaven have not been shared fairly. GDP per head in the Capital region is nearly twice that of the Northern region, where around 1 in 6 households live in relative poverty. Environmental groups warn that faster growth could increase carbon emissions and pressure on green space, as Norhaven still generates around 35% of its electricity from coal and gas. Supporters reply that faster growth would raise tax revenues, allowing more spending on public services and on the switch to renewable energy, and would create better-paid jobs.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Actual growth is an increase in real GDP (the output actually produced), which can come from using spare capacity. Potential growth is an increase in the productive capacity of the economy (an outward shift of the PPF or a rightward shift of LRAS), caused by increases in the quantity or quality of factors of production.
Application: Real GDP per head 2015 = £400 billion / 20.0 million = £20,000. 2025 = £442 billion / 21.2 million = about £20,849. Percentage change = (20,849 - 20,000) / 20,000 x 100 = about +4.2% (accept 4.2% to 4.3%) over ten years.
Analysis: Actual growth can exceed potential growth for a time while spare capacity is used up, but in the long run sustained growth requires potential growth. With unemployment down to 4.1%, Norhaven has little spare capacity, so further actual growth depends on raising productive capacity, especially productivity (output per hour up only 5%).
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for correct GDP per head in both years; 1 mark for +4.2% (accept 4.2% to 4.3%); 1 mark for defining actual growth; 1 mark for defining potential growth; 1 mark for application, for example linking low unemployment to the need for potential growth.

Knowledge: Gross investment is total spending on capital goods in a period; net investment is gross investment minus depreciation (capital consumption), and measures the addition to the capital stock.
Application: Net investment 2015 = £64 billion - £52 billion = £12 billion. Net investment 2025 = £68 billion - £61 billion = £7 billion (a fall of around 42%, from about 3% of GDP to about 1.6% of GDP), even though gross investment rose.
Analysis: Only net investment increases the capital stock; most of Norhaven's gross investment is simply replacing worn-out capital. With little growth in capital per worker (capital deepening), labour productivity grows slowly (output per hour up only 5%), so LRAS shifts right only slowly and potential growth is weak.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge (distinction between gross and net investment); 1 mark for £12 billion; 1 mark for £7 billion; up to 2 marks for explaining the link from net investment to the capital stock, productivity and LRAS or potential growth, using the data.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Labour productivity is output per worker or per hour worked. Determinants of LRAS: quantity and quality of capital, technology and innovation, education and skills (human capital), infrastructure, the efficiency of markets including planning rules.
Application: Output per hour up only 5% in ten years versus around 15% in trading partners; net investment fell from £12 billion to £7 billion; R&D at 0.9% of GDP; shortages of engineers, technicians and construction workers; slow, costly planning; poor transport links; only 27% of adults in the Northern region have higher qualifications compared with 52% in the Capital region.
Analysis: Factor 1, low net investment: little growth in capital per worker means workers use ageing equipment and cannot raise output per hour; low R&D means slower adoption of new technology, so productivity gains are limited. Factor 2, skills shortages: a lack of engineers and technicians limits firms' ability to use advanced technology, and workers with lower human capital produce less per hour; regional gaps in qualifications concentrate the problem. Alternative valid factors: planning rules restricting expansion of efficient firms; poor infrastructure raising transport costs and limiting market size. Each linked to slower rightward shifts of LRAS.
Evaluation: Relative importance: falling net investment is a measurable, sustained trend, whereas R&D changed little (1.0% to 0.9%), so investment may be the bigger factor. The factors interact: firms may not invest because they cannot find skilled workers. Low unemployment may mean less productive workers have been drawn into jobs, lowering average productivity (a composition effect). Productivity in services is hard to measure. Judgement.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis (KAA) up to 5 marks; Evaluation up to 3 marks.
Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
KAA Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but may be incomplete or one-sided, and diagrams may contain minor errors or not be explained.
KAA Level 3 (5 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context, using the data selectively; analysis develops clear, logical, multi-step chains of reasoning, supported by accurate diagrams integrated into the answer where relevant.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluative comments are generic, asserted or unsupported by evidence; no clear judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (3 marks): Relevant evaluation that is supported by evidence from the extracts or wider knowledge, weighing arguments and reaching a reasoned judgement.
A* answer: Develops two clearly distinct factors, each with a full chain from cause to output per hour to LRAS, uses figures from Table 1, Table 2 and Extract A, and evaluates by comparing the importance of the factors, recognising how they interact and noting measurement issues.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: AD = C + I + G + (X - M); a cut in income tax raises disposable income, increasing consumption and shifting AD right, with a multiplier effect; equilibrium real output where AD = AS; Keynesian LRAS becoming vertical near full capacity, or classical LRAS; supply-side incentives to work.
Application: Basic rate cut from 22% to 20%; unemployment only 4.1%; firms struggling to recruit; fiscal watchdog warns of added demand with little spare capacity; slow productivity growth.
Analysis: Demand side: higher disposable income raises consumption, shifting AD right; with the economy close to full capacity (the steep part of a Keynesian AS curve, or near LRAS), the main effect is a higher price level with only a small increase in real output (demand-pull inflation). Diagram: AD1 to AD2 near the vertical section, showing a large rise in the price level and small rise in real output. Supply side: higher post-tax wages increase the incentive to work and may raise participation and hours, shifting LRAS right over time, which allows real output to rise with less inflation.
Evaluation: The size of the AD shift depends on the marginal propensity to consume and import: if much of the extra income is saved or spent on imports, the effect is small. Supply-side incentive effects are uncertain: the income effect may lead some workers to work fewer hours. The cut benefits basic-rate taxpayers broadly, so it is poorly targeted at productivity. Time lags: the AD effect is quick while supply-side effects are slow, so inflationary pressure comes first. Classical economists would expect output to return to LRAS in the long run with only higher prices. Judgement.

Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
KAA Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but may be incomplete or one-sided, and diagrams may contain minor errors or not be explained.
KAA Level 3 (5-6 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context, using the data selectively; analysis develops clear, logical, multi-step chains of reasoning, supported by accurate diagrams integrated into the answer where relevant.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluative comments are generic, asserted or unsupported by evidence; no clear judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Relevant evaluation that is supported by evidence from the extracts or wider knowledge, weighing arguments and reaching a reasoned judgement.
A* answer: Draws an accurate AD/AS diagram showing the economy near full capacity, explains both the demand-side and supply-side chains, uses the 4.1% unemployment rate and the watchdog's warning, and evaluates through the size of the MPC and MPM, incentive effects and the timing of the two effects to reach a judgement on whether the main outcome is higher output or higher prices.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Benefits and costs of economic growth for consumers, firms, workers, the government, the environment and different regions; the distribution of income; the fiscal dividend; sustainability.
Application: GDP per head in the Capital region (£30,000) is nearly twice that of the Northern region (£16,500); around 1 in 6 Northern households in relative poverty; 35% of electricity from coal and gas; supporters' claims about tax revenue, public services and better-paid jobs; low unemployment (4.1%) and recruitment difficulties; real GDP per head up only around 4% in ten years.
Analysis: Consumers and workers: higher real incomes and more choice, better-paid jobs. Firms: higher sales and profits, encouraging investment (accelerator). Government: higher tax revenue and lower welfare spending (a fiscal dividend) to fund public services and renewable energy. Costs: if growth is concentrated in the Capital region, regional inequality widens and Northern households in poverty gain little; with fossil fuels supplying 35% of electricity, more output means more carbon emissions and loss of green space, imposing external costs on current and future generations; growth with little spare capacity may cause inflation, which hurts those on fixed incomes.
Evaluation: It depends on the source and type of growth: productivity growth driven by skills in the Northern and Coastal regions would spread benefits more widely than growth driven by the Capital region's financial sector. Green growth is possible if extra tax revenue funds renewables, decoupling growth from emissions. Short run versus long run: environmental costs may come first, benefits later. Policy matters: the government can redistribute gains through taxes and benefits. Judgement: growth is likely to benefit most groups on average but not all, unless accompanied by regional and environmental policies.

KAA Level 2 (3-5 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but may be incomplete or one-sided, and diagrams may contain minor errors or not be explained.

Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Relevant evaluation that is supported by evidence from the extracts or wider knowledge, weighing arguments and reaching a reasoned judgement.

questions.prompt: Evaluate whether the market-based supply-side policies in Extract B are likely to be more effective than the interventionist supply-side policies in raising productivity growth in Norhaven.

Extract A: Norhaven's productivity puzzle
Norhaven, a fictional economy, has grown steadily but slowly since 2015. Most of its growth has come from more people working rather than from each worker producing more: output per hour rose by only 5% in ten years, compared with around 15% in its main trading partners. Business surveys point to several causes. Net investment has been low, so many firms rely on ageing equipment; spending on research and development is below 1% of GDP; and employers report shortages of engineers, technicians and skilled construction workers. Planning rules make it slow and costly to build new factories, warehouses and homes, and transport links between the Northern region and the Capital region are poor. Unemployment is now low and firms say they are struggling to recruit.

Extract B: The Growth Plan
In its 2025 Budget the government announced a Growth Plan. Its market-based measures are: cutting the basic rate of income tax from 22% to 20%; cutting corporation tax from 28% to 25%; allowing firms to deduct the full cost of new machinery from taxable profits in the year it is bought; and simplifying planning rules. Its interventionist measures are: £3 billion a year for apprenticeships and technical colleges in the Northern and Coastal regions; a state-owned investment bank to lend to small firms; and £2 billion a year of extra public spending on research grants. The independent fiscal watchdog estimates that the plan will raise the economy's potential growth rate by between 0.2 and 0.4 percentage points a year after five years, but warns that the income tax cut will add to demand at a time when there is little spare capacity.

Extract C: Growth for whom?
Critics argue that the benefits of growth in Norhaven have not been shared fairly. GDP per head in the Capital region is nearly twice that of the Northern region, where around 1 in 6 households live in relative poverty. Environmental groups warn that faster growth could increase carbon emissions and pressure on green space, as Norhaven still generates around 35% of its electricity from coal and gas. Supporters reply that faster growth would raise tax revenues, allowing more spending on public services and on the switch to renewable energy, and would create better-paid jobs.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Supply-side policies aim to increase the productive capacity of the economy, shifting LRAS right. Market-based policies (tax cuts, deregulation) work by improving incentives and the operation of free markets; interventionist policies (state spending on education and training, infrastructure, R&D, state lending) involve the government directly correcting market failures.
Application: Income tax cut from 22% to 20%; corporation tax cut from 28% to 25%; full expensing of machinery; simpler planning rules; £3 billion a year on apprenticeships and technical colleges; state investment bank for small firms; £2 billion a year on research grants; watchdog estimate of +0.2 to +0.4 percentage points on potential growth after five years; net investment down to £7 billion; R&D at 0.9% of GDP; skills gaps by region; low unemployment.
Analysis: Market-based: lower corporation tax and full expensing raise the post-tax return on investment, so firms buy more machinery, increasing capital per worker and productivity; simpler planning allows efficient firms to expand and new factories to be built; the income tax cut improves work incentives. Interventionist: apprenticeships and technical colleges address skills shortages (a positive externality that firms underprovide because trained workers may leave), raising human capital in the regions where it is lowest; research grants correct the under-provision of R&D, which has positive spillovers; a state investment bank fills a gap in lending to small firms that private banks see as risky. Both shift LRAS right; diagram showing LRAS1 to LRAS2 with higher potential output at a lower price level.
Evaluation: Effectiveness depends on the cause of low productivity: if the main problems are skills and a lack of finance (market failures), interventionist policies target them directly; if it is weak incentives and regulation, market-based policies are more relevant. Deadweight: tax incentives reward investment that would have happened anyway; the income tax cut mainly boosts demand when there is little spare capacity, risking inflation rather than productivity. Government failure risks with interventionist measures: poor choice of training or projects, lending to unviable firms. Time lags: training and research take years to raise productivity, while planning reform and full expensing could act faster. Cost and opportunity cost: lower tax revenue versus £5 billion a year of spending. Equity: tax cuts benefit higher earners and the Capital region more; regional training spending targets disadvantaged areas. The modest watchdog estimate suggests neither is a quick fix. Prioritised judgement, for example: the measures are complements, but full expensing, planning reform and skills spending are likely to do more than the income tax cut.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis (KAA) up to 12 marks; Evaluation up to 8 marks.
Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-3 marks): Isolated knowledge, often limited to definitions; little or no application to the context; analysis is descriptive or confused.
KAA Level 2 (4-6 marks): Mostly accurate knowledge with some application to the context and data; chains of reasoning are partial or not clearly linked to the question; diagrams, if used, contain errors or are not explained.
KAA Level 3 (7-9 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with relevant use of data from the extracts; several developed chains of reasoning, though some lack depth or balance; diagrams are mostly accurate and referred to.
KAA Level 4 (10-12 marks): Precise, wide-ranging knowledge applied throughout, integrating data from the extracts; fully developed, coherent chains of reasoning covering both sides of the issue; accurate diagrams are integrated into the argument.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-3 marks): Evaluative comments are generic or asserted, with little reference to the context; no supported judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (4-6 marks): Evaluation addresses relevant issues with some support from the extracts, but is not fully developed, not prioritised or lacks a clear final judgement.
Evaluation Level 3 (7-8 marks): Sustained, well-supported evaluation that weighs the arguments, prioritises the most significant factors, recognises what the answer depends on and reaches a fully justified judgement.
A* answer: Explains the mechanisms of specific market-based and interventionist measures from Extract B with an LRAS diagram, links each to a cause of low productivity identified in Extract A and the tables, evaluates both types through deadweight, government failure, time lags, cost, demand-side side effects and equity, and reaches a clear, prioritised judgement rather than treating the two approaches as simple opposites.
